slides.title: Parallel Computing with `multiprocessing`
slides.prompt: The `multiprocessing` module side-steps the GIL by creating independent Python subprocesses, each with its own memory space and Python interpreter instance. `multiprocessing.Pool` offers easy parallel function execution.
slides.codeSnippet:
from multiprocessing import Pool

def square(x):
    return x * x

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Distribute computations across process pool
    with Pool(processes=4) as pool:
        results = pool.map(square, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
        print(results)  # [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]

slides.title: Process Protection Guard
slides.prompt: Why is `if __name__ == '__main__':` mandatory when launching multiprocessing tasks in Python, especially on Windows?
options: To prevent infinite recursive process spawning during child process import execution
To allow the GIL to bypass administrative system security checks
To ensure all variables are converted to global scope before execution
To mark memory as read-only for multi-core processors
slides.correctAnswer: To prevent infinite recursive process spawning during child process import execution

slides.title: Memory Sharing in Multiprocessing
slides.prompt: How does memory allocation in `multiprocessing` differ from `threading`?
options: Multiprocessing isolates memory per process; threads share the process heap memory
Multiprocessing shares all heap variables; threads run in isolated virtual spaces
Both share exact memory locations with zero copy overhead
Multiprocessing stores memory on disk rather than RAM
slides.correctAnswer: Multiprocessing isolates memory per process; threads share the process heap memory
